name: East Boston
headline: Former harbor islands joined by landfill,
with five Blue Line stops, Piers Park and Logan Airport on the water.
answer: East Boston is a Boston neighborhood across Boston Harbor from downtown, built on several former islands joined by landfill and laid out on a street grid by the East Boston Company from 1833. The Boston Planning Department counted 43,066 residents there in 2020. Its housing runs from 1840s Greek Revival brick houses on Jeffries Point to Italianate and Second Empire houses on Eagle Hill, and the Blue Line stops at Maverick, Airport, Wood Island, Orient Heights and Suffolk Downs.
meta: East Boston: former harbor islands laid out on a grid from 1833, with Jeffries Point and Eagle Hill, five Blue Line stops, Piers Park and 2025 Warren Group prices.

boundaries.text: East Boston lies across Boston Harbor to the northeast of downtown, separated from Charlestown and downtown by the harbor and bordering Winthrop, Revere and Chelsea. Logan International Airport occupies much of its eastern side.

overview: East Boston was built on Noddle's Island, the largest of five islands (with Hog, Governor's, Bird and Apple) that landfill later joined into one landmass, including the ground under Logan Airport. The island was farmed through the 1700s. In 1833 William H. Sumner, with Steven White and Francis J. Oliver, formed the East Boston Company, which by 1834 controlled the island and laid it out on a grid of streets, the first planned neighborhood in Boston. Donald McKay opened his shipyard on Border Street in 1845, and his clipper Flying Cloud, launched in 1851, twice sailed from New York to San Francisco in 89 days. Shipbuilding became the mainstay of the local economy.

The oldest streets are on Jeffries Point, at the southern end facing downtown, where Belmont Square (now Brophy Memorial Park) on Camp Hill survives from the original plan and is edged by brick bowfront houses built around 1847 to 1852. Eagle Hill to the north has a National Register historic district of houses built roughly between 1834 and 1900. Maverick Square and Central Square are the main commercial areas. Transportation reshaped the neighborhood through the 20th century: the East Boston streetcar tunnel, now the Blue Line, opened in 1904 as the first underwater tunnel in North America; the airfield that became Logan opened on September 8, 1923; and rows of houses were cleared for the Sumner Tunnel (opened June 30, 1934) and the Callahan Tunnel (1961). The Ted Williams Tunnel brought I-90 to East Boston in 1995.

Recent planning has covered both the established neighborhood and its largest open site. The Boston Planning & Development Agency board adopted PLAN: East Boston on January 18, 2024, after work that began in 2018; it covers roughly two square miles, excluding Logan Airport and the Suffolk Downs site, and the zoning amendments to Article 53 that carry it out were adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission on April 24, 2024. At the former Suffolk Downs racetrack, whose last day of live racing was June 30, 2019, the agency approved in September 2020 a redevelopment of the 161-acre site in East Boston and Revere with 10,000 housing units and almost three million square feet of office and retail space. On the waterfront, Massport opened a 4.5-acre second phase of Piers Park in December 2023.

housing.text: East Boston's housing includes Greek Revival brick bowfront houses of about 1847 to 1852 on Belmont Square, Greek Revival, Italianate and mansard double houses on Jeffries Point (where most residential building came between 1840 and 1890), and Italianate, Second Empire and Renaissance Revival houses in the Eagle Hill historic district. The Boston Planning & Development Agency's tabulation of the 2016-2020 American Community Survey counts 17,123 occupied housing units, 25.6% of them owner-occupied and 74.4% renter-occupied.

areas.name: Jeffries Point
areas.line: The earliest-settled part of East Boston, at the southern end facing downtown, developed by the East Boston Company from 1833; nine Greek Revival brick bowfront houses at 177 to 193 Webster Street line Belmont Square (Brophy Memorial Park) on Camp Hill.

areas.name: Eagle Hill
areas.line: A National Register historic district, listed on February 26, 1998, roughly bounded by Meridian, Princeton and White Streets meeting in Prescott Square, with mostly Italianate, Second Empire and Renaissance Revival buildings from about 1834 to 1900.

areas.name: Maverick Square
areas.line: One of East Boston's two main commercial areas, with Central Square, and the site of the Blue Line's Maverick station, opened on April 18, 1924.

areas.name: Orient Heights
areas.line: The northern part of the neighborhood, with Constitution Beach facing the runways of Logan Airport and the Orient Heights Blue Line station, opened on January 5, 1952.

commute.text: The Blue Line runs under the harbor from Maverick to downtown and stops at five stations in East Boston: Maverick, Airport, Wood Island, Orient Heights and Suffolk Downs. Massport runs free shuttle buses from Airport station to the Logan terminals. The MBTA's seasonal East Boston Ferry links Lewis Mall with Long Wharf. East Boston has no commuter rail station. I-90 reaches it through the Ted Williams Tunnel, and Route 1A through the Sumner and Callahan Tunnels.

places.name: Piers Park
places.line: A Massport park on the southwest side of East Boston facing downtown: the 6.5-acre first phase opened in 1995 with a 600-foot brick promenade, four shade pavilions (one dedicated to Donald McKay) and the Piers Park Sailing Center, and a 4.5-acre second phase opened in December 2023.

places.name: Belle Isle Marsh Reservation
places.line: A DCR reservation at 1399 Bennington Street, Boston's largest remaining salt marsh, with accessible trails; open 6am to 5pm.

places.name: Constitution Beach
places.line: A public beach in Orient Heights with a bathhouse, playground, courts, ball fields and an indoor ice rink, looking directly onto Logan's runways 22L and 22R about 2,000 feet away.

places.name: East Boston Greenway
places.line: A path on a former Grand Junction Railroad freight line, opened in 2007, linking Piers Park, Memorial Stadium, Bremen Street Park, Wood Island Bay Marsh and Belle Isle Marsh; it is planned to run 3.3 miles when complete.

places.name: Bremen Street Park
places.line: A park on the Greenway with an entrance to the Blue Line's Airport station.

places.name: Belmont Square (Brophy Memorial Park)
places.line: A square on Camp Hill laid out in the East Boston Company's original plan, with harbor views, Greek Revival bowfront houses on Webster Street, and the Golden Stairs descending to Marginal Street at the water's edge.

places.name: Donald McKay House
places.line: The shipbuilder's house on White Street, a Boston Landmark since 1977 and listed on the National Register; it is a private residence.

history.text: William H. Sumner, Steven White and Francis J. Oliver founded the East Boston Company, which laid out Noddle's Island on a street grid.
Donald McKay opened his shipyard on Border Street, where the clipper Flying Cloud was launched in 1851.
The East Boston streetcar tunnel, now part of the Blue Line, opened on December 30 under the harbor.
Boston Air Port, now Logan International Airport, opened on September 8 at Jeffries Point.

'Moving to East Boston MA' was not searched.

faq.q: What is the median home price in East Boston?
faq.a: According to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town table, which lists East Boston on its own row, the median single-family sale price for calendar year 2025 was $649,000, across 41 sales, against $700,000 across 23 sales in 2024. The condominium median was $645,000 in 2025, across 263 sales, against $665,000 across 302 sales in 2024.

faq.q: Does East Boston have commuter rail?
faq.a: No. East Boston is served by the Blue Line at Maverick, Airport, Wood Island, Orient Heights and Suffolk Downs, and by the MBTA's seasonal East Boston Ferry from Lewis Mall to Long Wharf.

faq.q: Which school district serves East Boston?
faq.a: Boston Public Schools. School assignment is by address under the district's home-based assignment system; review the district's profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is planned for Suffolk Downs?
faq.a: In September 2020 the Boston Planning & Development Agency approved the redevelopment of the 161-acre former racetrack in East Boston and Revere with 10,000 housing units, including 930 income-restricted units on site, and almost three million square feet of office and retail space. Live racing ended on June 30, 2019.

A neighborhood-wide plan for land use, zoning, transportation and the public realm, adopted by the Boston Planning & Development Agency board on January 18, 2024. Its zoning amendments to Article 53 were adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission on April 24, 2024. It excludes Logan Airport and the Suffolk Downs site.

notes: Written 2026-10-23. Population: 43,066 from the Boston Planning & Development Agency (now Boston Planning Department) Research Division '2020 U.S. Census Redistricting Data Release', table 'Boston Adult and Child Populations', row 'East Boston 43,066 6.4% 34,826 80.9% 8,240 19.1%', which uses consistent 2020 tract-defined neighborhood boundaries (same source and method as charlestown.json). The same release's housing units row is 'East Boston 18,016 16,695 92.7% 1,321 7.3%' (not used in the text). The PLAN: East Boston page says the plan area is 'home to more than 47,000 residents'; that is a different, later figure and boundary and is not used. Housing tenure from the BPDA 'Boston in Context: Neighborhoods' (April 2022), Housing Tenure row 'East Boston 17,123 93.0% 4,380 25.6% 12,743 74.4%' (ACS 2016-2020). Housing types: Belmont Square bowfronts (177 to 193 Webster Street, Benjamin Lamson, about 1847 to 1852) from SAH Archipedia; Jeffries Point 1840 to 1890 and mansard double houses from the Boston Preservation Alliance's East Boston neighborhood preservation report (https://bostonpreservation.org/sites/default/files/2018-05/EASTBOSTONFINALNPPREPORT%20%281%29.pdf); Eagle Hill styles and NRHP date from Wikipedia. No source opened this session gave triple-decker or wood-frame counts for East Boston, so triple-deckers are not claimed as a type. Islands, East Boston Company (1833, grid 1834, 'first planned neighborhood in Boston'), McKay's 1845 shipyard, 1904 tunnel 'first underwater tunnel in North America', 1934 and 1961 house clearances, 1995 Ted Williams Tunnel, Massport shuttles and the borders with Winthrop, Revere and Chelsea from Wikipedia's East Boston article. Wikipedia's article also says East Boston was 'annexed to Boston' in 1836; Noddle's Island's own article gives no annexation date, so no annexation year is given. Sumner Tunnel June 30, 1934 and Callahan 1961 from Wikipedia's Sumner Tunnel article; Logan September 8, 1923 at Jeffries Point from Wikipedia. Blue Line station dates (Maverick April 18, 1924; Orient Heights January 5, 1952; tunnel December 30, 1904) from Wikipedia's Blue Line article; Beachmont is in Revere and is not listed. Ferry name and stops from https://www.mbta.com/schedules/Boat-EastBoston, marked 'Seasonal Service'; its start date was not confirmed. PLAN: East Boston dates, area and Article 53 from https://www.bostonplans.org/planning/planning-initiatives/plan-east-boston. Suffolk Downs: last live racing June 30, 2019 (Wikipedia); 161 acres, 10,000 units, 930 on-site affordable units and almost three million square feet from the East Boston Times (September 29, 2020), which says the BPDA approved it 'last Thursday' (so September 24, 2020; the record says only September 2020). The BPDA project page could not be opened, and the East Boston and Revere shares of the site and units were not confirmed. Piers Park phases and features from Wikipedia (Massport ownership); Phase III (proposed, 3.8 acres) left out. Belle Isle Marsh address, hours and description from mass.gov; acreage not given there and left out. Constitution Beach facilities and runway distance from Wikipedia; the mass.gov page failed to load, so DCR management is not claimed. Greenway: Wikipedia says it opened in 2007 and will be 3.3 miles when complete; the 2019 renaming to the Mary Ellen Welch Greenway appears in Wikipedia's East Boston article but not the Greenway article, so it is left out. McKay House: Boston Landmark 1977 and NRHP from Wikipedia's Donald McKay article; the street (White Street) and its use as a two-family residence from the Boston Preservation Alliance report. Maverick Square and Central Square as main commercial areas, and the islands-and-landfill description, from the bostonplans.org East Boston page. Schools: Boston Public Schools (DESE orgcode 00350000); assignment is by address and set by the district under its Home-Based policy for kindergarten through grade 8, which gives each family a choice list built from its home address (https://www.bostonpublicschools.org/assignment); no individual school is named or described. Region is 'Greater Boston' as instructed for this round (the Charlestown and South Boston records use 'Greater Boston (the city)'). Fair housing: left out Wikipedia's demographic and ancestry sections, the statement that Orient Heights was the first area in Massachusetts settled by Italian immigrants, the immigration station history framed by national origin, SAH Archipedia's description of the parish as serving particular immigrant groups and of population change, Piers Park's Commons Pavilion description as a tribute to 'immigrant history', and Wikipedia's mention of Logan expansion displacing 'families'. Suffolk Downs and the housing figures are described by units and square footage, not by who will live there.
